e.etymology: The spelling of Esther used in Spanish, Portuguese, Italian and the Scandinavian languages. Esther is the Jewish queen of Persia in the Bible; her name is often linked to a Persian word for star.

assoc.t: ester, a class of compounds in organic chemistry

e.etymology: From Arabic, a feminine name built on the root of zayn, beauty or adornment, which also gives Zain and Zainab.
In English a spelling of Kristin, from Christina, a follower of Christ. In Denmark and Norway Kristen is a men's name, a form of Christian. It peaked for American girls in the early 1980s.
namesakes: Kristen Bell (actress and the voice of Anna in Frozen)

e.etymology: The anglicized spelling of Irish Séamas, the Irish form of James. James comes through Latin Iacomus from the Hebrew name Jacob, traditionally read as supplanter or holder of the heel.
A combination of Lily, the flower name, and Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace. It sounds the same as the older name Liliana.
The Hebrew word for bear. It is the Hebrew partner of the Yiddish name Ber, and the two are often paired as Dov Ber.
From Arabic Na'ila, built on a root meaning to attain or obtain and commonly glossed as gracious or successful.
The Portuguese form of David, from Hebrew Dawid, beloved. Davi is one of the most popular boys' names in Brazil.
The Spanish form of Noelle, from French Noël, Christmas, which goes back to Latin natalis, of a birth. It is often given to girls born near Christmas.
From Arabic ayat, the plural of aya, a sign or miracle and the word for a verse of the Quran.
A respelling of the English word story, from Latin historia by way of Old French. Story joined Lyric, Poet and Journey as a word name in the 2000s.
From Arabic samiya, exalted or sublime, the feminine of Sami. In the US it took off in the 2000s alongside Aaliyah and Saniyah.
Made known by Finnick Odair, the trident-wielding victor in Suzanne Collins's Hunger Games novels of 2009 and 2010. As a given name it reads as a longer form of Finn.
namesakes: Finnick Odair (District 4 victor in The Hunger Games)

assoc.t: Finnick Odair of The Hunger Games
Finnick, the fennec fox in Disney's Zootopia

e.meaning: settlement where beans or bent grass grow
e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English bean, bean, or beonet, bent grass, plus tun, an enclosure or settlement. It was most used as a first name in the 1880s.
A modern American name that joins Jazz, from Jasmine or the music, to the -lyn ending. It is one of many spellings alongside Jazlyn and Jaslyn.
From Sanskrit viraj, shining forth or ruling far and wide. In Vedic texts Viraj is a name for the primal creative power of the universe.
A Spanish phonetic spelling of the English name Amy, which comes from Old French Amee, beloved. It is used mostly in Latin American and US Hispanic families.

From Greek Sibylla, the title of the prophetesses of the ancient world. Christians accepted the name in the Middle Ages because the sibyls were thought to have foretold Christ; Sybil has been the usual spelling since the 1800s.
namesakes: Lady Sybil Crawley (youngest daughter on Downton Abbey)
Sybil Fawlty (Basil's wife on Fawlty Towers)
Sybil Ludington (teenage rider of the American Revolution)

assoc.t: Sybil, 1970s book and film about multiple personalities

e.note: Older Americans may connect it with Sybil, the famous 1970s case of multiple personality disorder.

e.etymology: The Italian original of Francis, from Medieval Latin Franciscus, Frenchman or Frank. It began as the nickname of Saint Francis of Assisi, whose father traded in France, and is among the commonest names in Italy.
namesakes: Francesco Bernoulli (Italian race car in Pixar's Cars 2)

e.etymology: A name of Mexican and Mexican American families, close in form to Adelina and Adeline.
A recent American name with the sound of Kai, Zakai and Malakai. Kasai is also a river and region of central Africa and a Japanese surname.
A 20th-century spelling of Laurie, a pet form of Laura, from Latin laurus, laurel. It is also short for Loretta and Lorraine. Lori was a top American girls' name of the 1960s.
An English place name and surname from Old English clif, cliff or steep bank, plus ford, a river crossing. It was a popular first name from the 1880s through the 1930s.
namesakes: Clifford the Big Red Dog (children's book and TV character)

assoc.t: Clifford the Big Red Dog of children's books and TV

e.note: Children and parents alike will think of Clifford the Big Red Dog.

e.meaning: of Delos, the birthplace of Artemis
e.etymology: From Greek Delia, an epithet of the goddess Artemis, who was born on the island of Delos. It is also used as a short form of Adelia, Cordelia and Bedelia.
namesakes: Delia Owens (author of Where the Crawdads Sing)

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Deborah, from devorah, bee. In the Book of Judges Deborah is a prophetess and judge who leads Israel to victory. This spelling is usual in Jewish families.
The Danish and Norwegian spelling of Axel, a medieval Scandinavian form of the Biblical name Absalom, from Hebrew Avshalom, father of peace.
A modern spelling of Emily influenced by Lee. Emily comes from the Roman family name Aemilius, linked to Latin aemulus, rival.
Recorded as a girls' name of Persian origin; Sanai was also the pen name of a 12th-century Persian poet. In the US it sits alongside Sanaa and Saniyah and dates from the 2000s.
A spelling of Taj, the Persian and Arabic word for crown, as in the Taj Mahal. Use in the US rose in the late 1990s with actor Tahj Mowry, star of the sitcom Smart Guy.
namesakes: Tahj Mowry (actor, star of Smart Guy)

e.etymology: A modern American blend, explained as Jacob plus Corey, that fits with Ja- names such as Jakari and Jamari.
A modern spelling of Kendall, an English surname from the town of Kendal in Cumbria, whose name means valley of the River Kent.
